At the height of the Trump trade war with China, tariffs were announced almost weekly, prompting companies like Logitech to significantly raise prices on their US products.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. Yet no company has been seen passing those refunds on to consumers, and class action lawsuits have been filed along these lines...

Trump tariff saga

Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China last year, clearly believing that slapping higher tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move production back to the US.

But of course that never happened. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, and cheap labor needed to produce consumer electronics at the scale major brands require.

Trump insisted China was paying the tariffs, but the reality is that it was US brands importing finished products that paid them, and the increased costs were ultimately passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the peak of the saga, tariff rates had soared to 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by as much as 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose those tariffs unilaterally, and ordered refunds to US businesses—a process that is now underway.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and none of the affected companies have indicated any intention to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech on this basis, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

The principle is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to consumers, and are now getting refunds from the government. Morally speaking, companies ought to return that money to consumers who bought their products during that period.

In practical execution, however, it's extremely difficult. Logitech would need to verify every transaction made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track what consumers actually paid, and calculate how much of that was attributable to tariffs.

If this lawsuit succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent—though it's worth noting that in class actions, it's usually the lawyers who benefit most, while the average payout to consumers tends to be fairly limited.
